papers.full_text: Angiopoietin-1/Tie2 Activation as a Therapeutic Hypothesis for 1 Hantavirus-Induced Vascular Permeability 2 Author: Atharv Dhore1 3 Affiliation: 1 Aldie, Virginia, USA 4 † Corresponding author: Atharv Dhore, anish.dhore@gmail.com 5 Abstract 6 Severe hantavirus infection produces extensive vascular leakage, driven by a combination of endothelial 7 dysfunction, dysregulated inflammation, VEGF-mediated hyperpermeability, angiopoietin imbalance, and 8 degradation of the endothelial glycocalyx. This narrative review draws on the peer-reviewed literature, with 9 particular attention to work published between 2016 and 2026, to examine how hantavirus-induced vascular 10 permeability arises in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), 11 and how Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1)/Tie2 signaling and glycocalyx injury contribute to endothelial barrier failure. 12 Direct hantavirus evidence shows that Ang-1 inhibits hantavirus-directed endothelial permeability in vitro and that 13 angiopoietin dysregulation tracks with disease severity in patients; findings that Tie2 activation curbs vascular 14 leakage in sepsis and other non-hantavirus models are mechanistically suggestive but remain inferential rather than 15 hantavirus-specific. No hantavirus animal model or clinical trial has yet evaluated Ang-1/Tie2-directed therapy, so 16 this review treats the approach as a testable hypothesis rather than an established or recommended treatment; 17 confirming its therapeutic value will require dedicated hantavirus-specific animal and clinical studies. 18 Keywords: hantavirus, endothelial dysfunction, vascular permeability, angiopoietin; Tie2, therapeutic hypothesis 19 1. Introduction 20 Hantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae. They persist in chronically infected rodent 21 reservoirs (and, in a few species, shrews or moles) and reach humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized 22 excreta. The Old World hantaviruses, among them Hantaan virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava-Belgrade virus, 23 circulate across Europe and Asia and cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The New World 24 hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus, circulate throughout the Americas and cause hantavirus 25 pulmonary syndrome (HPS); Andes virus is unusual among hantaviruses in that it can also spread person-to-person.1 26 Both syndromes share a core clinical picture, increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, hypotension, and 27 multiorgan dysfunction, but differ in which organs bear the brunt of disease: HFRS chiefly affects the kidneys, while 28 HPS chiefly affects the lungs and heart, reflecting differences in which vascular beds each viral group preferentially 29 colonizes. Hantaviruses infect endothelial cells without lysing them outright; disease severity instead tracks with 30 disruption of endothelial barrier function.2 When that barrier fails badly enough, the result is pulmonary edema, 31 shock, renal failure, and death. 32 The two syndromes also differ sharply in how often they occur and how deadly they are. HFRS accounts for an 33 estimated 150,000-200,000 cases annually, most of them in Asia and Europe, with case fatality ranging from under 34 1% to roughly 15% depending on the causative virus.26 HPS is comparatively rare, with roughly 200 cases reported 35 each year across the Americas, but it carries a substantially higher case fatality rate of up to 50%. Neither syndrome 36 yet has an approved antiviral therapy or vaccine. This asymmetry (HFRS common but comparatively survivable, 37 HPS rare but often fatal) resurfaces throughout this review, since the direct clinical evidence bearing on the Ang- 38 1/Tie2 hypothesis is itself unevenly distributed between the two conditions. 39 The vascular leakage seen in hantavirus infection arises from an interplay of viral infection, inflammatory cytokines, 40 vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, angiopoietin dysregulation, and glycocalyx degradation.3 41 Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) is an endothelial-stabilizing ligand that activates the Tie2 receptor tyrosine kinase, 42 promoting endothelial quiescence, reinforcing the barrier, and dampening inflammatory signaling.4 Angiopoietin-2 43 (Ang-2) works in the opposite direction, destabilizing the vessel wall. 44 This paper is a narrative literature review that builds toward a therapeutic hypothesis, not an original experimental or 45 clinical study. It traces the molecular mechanisms behind hantavirus-induced endothelial dysfunction, with emphasis 46 on VEGF signaling, Ang-1/Tie2 pathway activity, IL-6 trans-signaling, angiopoietin imbalance, and glycocalyx 47 degradation, while distinguishing evidence gathered directly from hantavirus systems from evidence inferred from 48 related conditions such as sepsis and dengue. Sections 3 through 6 work through each mechanistic pathway in turn; 49 Section 7 draws this evidence together into an explicit direct-versus-inferential summary (Table 1) and lays out 50 concrete next steps and candidate experimental systems; Sections 8 and 9 address the review's limitations and state 51 its overall hypothesis. The central question is whether endothelial stabilization through Ang-1/Tie2 signaling, 52 together with the related pathways discussed alongside it, is a biologically plausible direction for hantavirus 53 research, while keeping hantavirus-specific evidence clearly separated from evidence borrowed from other diseases. 54 2. Literature Review Methodology 55 This review relies on a narrative approach to develop a therapeutic hypothesis. It is not a systematic review or meta- 56 analysis; a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram was not used, since the aim was to synthesize mechanistic and clinical 57 evidence rather than to pool results exhaustively. No original experiments, patient data, animal studies, or clinical 58 trial data were generated for this manuscript. 59 Literature was identified through structured searches of three databases, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of 60 Science, conducted on July 23, 2026 and restricted to English-language, peer-reviewed sources. The following 61 title/abstract/keyword search strings were used, combined with Boolean AND/OR operators: 62 1. ("hantavirus" OR "orthohantavirus" OR "Puumala virus" OR "Hantaan virus" OR "Andes virus" OR "Sin 63 Nombre virus") AND ("vascular permeability" OR "endothelial dysfunction" OR "capillary leak") 64 2. ("hantavirus" OR "hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome" OR "HFRS" OR "hantavirus pulmonary syndrome" 65 OR "HPS") AND ("angiopoietin" OR "Tie2" OR "Ang-1" OR "Ang-2") 66 3. ("hantavirus") AND ("VEGF" OR "vascular endothelial growth factor" OR "VE-cadherin") 67 4. ("hantavirus" OR "HFRS" OR "HPS") AND ("glycocalyx" OR "syndecan" OR "heparan sulfate") 68 5. ("angiopoietin" OR "Tie2 agonist" OR "vasculotide") AND ("sepsis" OR "acute lung injury" OR "dengue") AND 69 ("vascular leak" OR "endothelial permeability") 70 Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance to hantavirus pathogenesis, endothelial or vascular biology, and 71 angiopoietin/Tie2/glycocalyx signaling; full texts of potentially relevant records were then examined. 72 Records were included if they were peer-reviewed original research or review articles addressing (a) hantavirus 73 clinical disease or pathogenesis, (b) endothelial barrier or vascular permeability mechanisms relevant to VEGF, 74 angiopoietin/Tie2, or glycocalyx biology, or (c) Tie2-agonist or endothelial-stabilizing interventions in any disease 75 model, the last of these retained specifically to support explicitly labeled inferential, non-hantavirus, mechanistic 76 claims. 77 Records were excluded if they were non-peer-reviewed (news articles, general websites, blog posts), conference 78 abstracts without an accompanying peer-reviewed publication, or of unclear or unverifiable peer-review status. 79 The initial exploratory search considered literature published between 1996 and 2026, but the reference base for this 80 manuscript emphasizes peer-reviewed sources from 2016 to 2026. A small number of earlier, foundational studies 81 are retained regardless, for example the 2008 in vitro demonstration that Ang-1 inhibits hantavirus-directed 82 endothelial permeability,6 the 2000 report that Ang-1 protects the adult vasculature against plasma leakage,11 and the 83 2013 identification of kallikrein-kinin system activation in hantavirus-infected endothelium,21 because they remain 84 the primary direct evidence for specific mechanistic claims and no more recent hantavirus-specific study has 85 superseded them. Each pre-2016 source retained on this basis is flagged as such at its first mention in the text. 86 The final evidence base comprises 26 references (see References). Throughout, this review distinguishes findings 87 obtained directly in hantavirus-infected cells, animals, or patients (direct evidence) from findings obtained in non- 88 hantavirus systems such as sepsis or dengue that are mechanistically relevant but untested in hantavirus infection 89 (inferential evidence); this distinction is flagged at each relevant claim in Sections 3-7 and summarized in Table 1. 90 3. Hantavirus Pathogenesis and Endothelial Dysfunction 91 Hantaviruses target the vascular endothelial cells lining capillaries and small blood vessels by binding beta-3 92 integrins, an interaction that facilitates viral entry and reshapes intracellular signaling.5 Beta-3 integrins normally 93 restrain VEGFR2 signaling and so act as negative regulators of VEGF-driven permeability; pathogenic hantaviruses 94 disable this restraint, and the resulting loss of integrin-mediated control is the proposed link between hantavirus 95 infection and the VEGF hyperresponsiveness discussed in Section 4. Even as the virus replicates successfully inside 96 endothelial cells, those cells remain structurally intact, so the vascular leakage that follows reflects altered 97 endothelial function rather than direct viral cytotoxicity. This distinguishes hantavirus-induced vascular leak from 98 the cytolytic viral hemorrhagic fevers and supports pursuing host-response-directed therapy alongside antiviral 99 approaches. 100 Capillary leakage and endothelial dysfunction underlie the clinical picture in both HFRS and HPS. As vascular 101 permeability rises, plasma and cells escape into surrounding tissue, producing pulmonary edema, hypovolemia, 102 hypotension, and organ dysfunction.3 Immune activation contributes substantially to disease severity, particularly 103 through cytokine-driven endothelial activation, discussed in detail in Section 3.1. The kallikrein-kinin system also 104 contributes directly to hantavirus-induced permeability: infected endothelial cells show increased factor XII and 105 kallikrein activity along with bradykinin release, and bradykinin in turn promotes vasodilation and vascular 106 permeability in this setting.21 107 3.1 Cytokine-Driven Endothelial Activation: IL-6 Trans-Signaling 108 Direct hantavirus evidence ties elevated cytokines to endothelial dysfunction and disease severity. In a cohort of 64 109 patients hospitalized with acute Puumala virus infection, serum IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and TGF-β1 were 110 significantly elevated relative to healthy controls, both early and late in the course of acute disease.23 IL-6 has since 111 emerged as a biomarker of HFRS and HPS severity, though until recently the mechanism linking it to endothelial 112 barrier failure was unclear. 113 A 2025 study closed that gap. IL-6 signals through two distinct routes: classical signaling, generally protective and 114 dependent on a membrane-bound IL-6 receptor that endothelial cells largely lack, and trans-signaling, mediated by a 115 soluble IL-6 receptor (sIL-6R) paired with the ubiquitous gp130 co-receptor, which can drive pathogenic responses 116 even in receptor-poor cell types such as endothelium. Using primary human endothelial cells infected with Puumala 117 virus and treated with recombinant sIL-6R, the study found that infection stimulates IL-6 secretion and that IL-6 118 trans-signaling, not classical signaling, drives endothelial barrier dysfunction in vitro. In plasma from 28 patients 119 with acute PUUV-associated HFRS, IL-6 trans-signaling potential correlated with markers of clinical severity, 120 including serum creatinine and thrombocytopenia.22 This is, to date, the most direct mechanistic link between a 121 hantavirus-elevated cytokine and endothelial barrier failure demonstrated in both an infected-cell system and 122 hantavirus patients, and it identifies IL-6 trans-signaling as a fourth hantavirus-validated pathway relevant to 123 endothelial-stabilizing therapy, alongside VEGF, Ang-1/Tie2, and glycocalyx degradation. As with the angiopoietin 124 data discussed in Section 5, however, this direct clinical evidence comes specifically from PUUV-associated HFRS 125 and has not yet been established for HPS. 126 4. VEGF-Mediated Endothelial Hyperpermeability 127 Vascular endothelial growth factor is a potent regulator of endothelial permeability.7 VEGF binds VEGFR2 on 128 endothelial cells and activates Src-family kinases that disrupt adherens junction proteins, including vascular 129 endothelial (VE)-cadherin.8 Loss of VE-cadherin weakens endothelial junctions and raises paracellular permeability. 130 Pathogenic hantaviruses sensitize endothelial cells to VEGF-induced permeability, so that infected cells respond far 131 more strongly to VEGF stimulation than uninfected ones.9 VEGF-driven phosphorylation of VE-cadherin widens 132 endothelial gaps and increases plasma leakage, and infected endothelial cells progressively downregulate VE- 133 cadherin in response.10 134 Unlike the angiopoietin and IL-6 trans-signaling evidence discussed in Sections 5 and 3.1, direct clinical evidence 135 for VEGF-driven permeability spans both hantavirus syndromes rather than just one. In HFRS, serum VEGF is 136 elevated and correlates with reduced soluble VEGFR2 during the acute phase of Hantaan virus infection.9 In HPS, 137 VEGF is similarly elevated in pulmonary edema fluid and peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with 138 acute Andes-virus-associated disease.24 Of the four mechanisms reviewed here (VEGF, Ang-1/Tie2, glycocalyx, IL- 139 6), VEGF is therefore the only one with direct human evidence in both HFRS and HPS, giving it broader direct 140 support than the other pathways discussed (Table 1). 141 5. Angiopoietin-1/Tie2 Signaling Pathway 142 The angiopoietin-Tie2 pathway governs endothelial stability and vascular integrity. Ang-1 binds and activates the 143 Tie2 receptor tyrosine kinase on endothelial cells, clustering Tie2 at cell-cell junctions and triggering downstream 144 PI3K/Akt signaling; this cascade phosphorylates and inactivates the forkhead transcription factor FOXO1, stabilizes 145 junctional complexes, supports endothelial survival and tight junction maintenance, sets anti-inflammatory signaling 146 in motion, and suppresses vascular leakage.4 Consistent with this broader vascular-protective role, Ang-1 has been 147 shown to protect the adult vasculature against plasma leakage,11 and, in direct hantavirus evidence from an in vitro 148 permeability assay, Ang-1 significantly inhibits hantavirus-directed endothelial permeability at physiologic 149 concentrations.6 150 Ang-2 works against this system, destabilizing blood vessels and antagonizing Tie2 signaling. Endothelial cells 151 release Ang-2 rapidly from Weibel-Palade bodies during inflammation and infection,13 and elevated Ang-2 152 promotes endothelial activation and greater vascular leak. In direct clinical hantavirus evidence, a cohort of 31 153 patients with acute Puumala virus infection and one patient with Dobrava-Belgrade (Sochi) virus infection showed 154 an elevated Ang-2/Ang-1 ratio relative to controls, and this imbalance correlated with markers of disease severity, 155 including serum creatinine and thrombocyte levels.12 An important caveat applies here: both patient groups 156 contributing this direct clinical evidence had HFRS rather than HPS, and no comparable human angiopoietin dataset 157 yet exists for HPS. Angiopoietin imbalance is not unique to hantavirus infection; similar Ang-2-driven vascular 158 instability has been described across other host-response-mediated inflammatory syndromes, which lends inferential 159 support to host-directed endothelial stabilization across inflammatory vascular leak syndromes generally, though it 160 remains inferential rather than direct hantavirus evidence.20 161 Tie2-targeting therapeutics have shown efficacy in non-hantavirus experimental models of vascular leak. In murine 162 sepsis, Tie2 activation reduces cytokine elevation, glycocalyx degradation, vascular leakage, and organ damage, a 163 finding from a sepsis model, not a hantavirus one.14 Vasculotide, a synthetic Tie2 agonist peptide, similarly reduces 164 mortality and vascular permeability in murine sepsis models, again in a non-hantavirus system.15 These studies make 165 Tie2 activation a biologically plausible endothelial-stabilizing strategy, but neither vasculotide nor any other Tie2 166 agonist has yet been tested in a hantavirus model. 167 6. Glycocalyx Degradation and Endothelial Barrier Failure 168 The endothelial glycocalyx is a carbohydrate-rich layer coating endothelial cells, built from glycoproteins, 169 proteoglycans, syndecans, and glycosaminoglycans such as heparan sulfate and hyaluronan.16 It regulates vascular 170 permeability, mechanotransduction, leukocyte adhesion, and plasma protein retention; when it is damaged, 171 endothelial permeability rises and vascular leak syndromes worsen. 172 Inflammation, oxidative stress, cytokines, and angiopoietin dysregulation all induce glycocalyx shedding, largely by 173 activating matrix metalloproteinases and heparanase, which cleave membrane-bound proteoglyc…

analysis.background: Severe hantavirus infection leads to extensive vascular leakage via endothelial dysfunction, dysregulated inflammation, VEGF‑mediated hyperpermeability, angiopoietin imbalance, and glycocalyx degradation. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: The review surveys mechanisms of permeability in HFRS and HPS, emphasizing Ang‑1/Tie2 signaling, angiopoietin imbalance, VEGF, IL‑6 trans‑signaling, and glycocalyx injury, and proposes Ang‑1/Tie2 activation as a therapeutic concept. (A2)
analysis.current_state: In vitro hantavirus studies show Ang‑1 inhibits endothelial permeability, and patient data link angiopoietin dysregulation with disease severity; most evidence for Tie2‑mediated protection derives from non‑hantavirus models. (A3)
analysis.gaps: Tie2 activation data are largely inferential from sepsis or other diseases, and no hantavirus‑specific animal model or clinical trial has evaluated Ang‑1/Tie2‑directed therapy. (A4)
analysis.future_research: Dedicated hantavirus animal experiments and controlled clinical trials are needed to assess the safety and efficacy of Ang‑1/Tie2‑based interventions. (A5)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Severe hantavirus infection causes vascular leakage through endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, VEGF, angiopoietin imbalance, and glycocalyx loss. Main directions: The review examines HFRS/HPS permeability mechanisms, focusing on Ang‑1/Tie2 signaling and related pathways as a therapeutic hypothesis. Current state: Ang‑1 reduces hantavirus‑induced leak in vitro and angiopoietin dysregulation correlates with severity, but Tie2 evidence is mostly from other diseases. Gaps: Tie2 findings are inferential and no hantavirus‑specific animal or clinical studies exist for Ang‑1/Tie2 therapy. Future research: Conduct hantavirus‑specific animal studies and clinical trials to test Ang‑1/Tie2 activation.

papers.title_zh: Ang-1/Tie2 激活作为 汉坦病毒 引起的血管通透性的治疗假设

analysis_zh.background: 严重的汉坦病毒感染通过内皮功能障碍、炎症失调、VEGF介导的通透性增高、血管生成素失衡以及糖萼降解导致广泛的血管渗漏。(A1)
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述回顾了肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒肺综合征中通透性机制,重点关注Ang‐1/Tie2信号、血管生成素失衡、VEGF、IL‐6转导信号以及糖萼损伤,并提出激活Ang‐1/Tie2作为治疗概念。(A2)

papers.title: Large language models for hantavirus-related infectious disease risk communication during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak: an expert-rated comparative content analysis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health information, but their reliability in outbreak-related public health communication remains uncertain. Hantavirus communication is challenging because messages must balance avoidance of unnecessary alarm with prevention of false reassurance, particularly during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak. This comparative, cross-sectional, expert-rated content analysis evaluated responses generated by three non-Pro publicly accessible LLMs - ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude - to 150 predefined hantavirus-related questions. Questions covered official health authority/guideline-based information, expert/clinical practice issues and public frequently asked questions. Each question was submitted using a standard zero-shot prompt and a public health risk communication prompt, generating 900 responses. Three independent experts assessed accuracy, completeness, consistency, safety and actionability using a predefined rubric. Ratings were summarised descriptively, and inter-rater reliability was assessed using percentage agreement and Fleiss’ kappa. Overall, 568 of 900 responses (63.1%) were rated as completely correct and sufficient, 232 (25.8%) as mostly correct but incomplete, and 100 (11.1%) as partially correct or potentially misleading. No response was rated as completely incorrect or overtly harmful. Within this dataset, ChatGPT had numerically the highest proportion of completely correct responses (198/300, 66.0%) and the lowest proportion of misleading responses (28/300, 9.3%); however, these differences were interpreted descriptively rather than as evidence of model superiority. Gemini and Claude had completely correct response rates of 62.7% and 60.7%, respectively. In this dataset, the generic public health risk communication prompt did not change the aggregate expert-rated categorical distribution. Major publicly accessible LLMs generated a high proportion of correct or mostly correct hantavirus risk communication responses, but approximately one in nine responses was potentially misleading. These tools may support infectious disease and outbreak-related risk communication but should not be used as stand-alone sources for clinically complex or rapidly evolving guidance without expert oversight and official-source grounding. Not applicable.

analysis.background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health information, but their reliability in outbreak-related public health communication remains uncertain, especially for hantavirus where messages must avoid unnecessary alarm while preventing false reassurance during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak.
analysis.methods: A comparative, cross‑sectional, expert‑rated content analysis evaluated responses generated by three publicly accessible LLMs—ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude—to 150 predefined hantavirus‑related questions, using a standard zero‑shot prompt and a public health risk communication prompt to produce 900 responses; three independent experts assessed accuracy, completeness, consistency, safety, and actionability with a predefined rubric and inter‑rater reliability was measured by percentage agreement and Fleiss’ kappa.
analysis.results: Overall, 568 of 900 responses (63.1 %) were rated as completely correct and sufficient, 232 (25.8 %) as mostly correct but incomplete, and 100 (11.1 %) as partially correct or potentially misleading; no response was rated as completely incorrect or overtly harmful. ChatGPT had the highest proportion of completely correct responses (198/300, 66.0 %) and the lowest proportion of misleading responses (28/300, 9.3 %), while Gemini and Claude had correct rates of 62.7 % and 60.7 % respectively; the generic public health risk communication prompt did not alter the overall distribution.
analysis.contribution: The study shows that major publicly accessible LLMs can generate a high proportion of correct or mostly correct hantavirus risk‑communication responses, but about one in nine responses may be potentially misleading, indicating that these tools can support outbreak communication when used with expert oversight and official‑source grounding.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.summary_en: Background: LLMs are increasingly used for health information, but their reliability in outbreak-related public health communication remains uncertain, especially for hantavirus during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak. Methods: A comparative, cross‑sectional, expert‑rated content analysis evaluated responses from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude to 150 hantavirus questions, generating 900 responses via zero‑shot and risk‑communication prompts; experts assessed accuracy, completeness, consistency, safety, and actionability. Results: 63.1 % of responses were completely correct, 25.8 % mostly correct but incomplete, and 11.1 % potentially misleading; ChatGPT had the highest correct rate (66.0 %) and lowest misleading rate (9.3 %). Contribution: Major LLMs can support outbreak risk communication but should not replace expert oversight. Limitations: not reported.

papers.title: Hantavirus mutagenesis is impacted by mutagens and host antiviral proteins
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that infect humans with high fatality rates. We currently have a poor understanding of the processes that contribute to hantavirus mutagenesis and therefore the potential for viral adaptation. To understand the drivers of mutations in hantaviruses, we calculated and compared mutational spectra across 14 divergent hantavirus species. We found that mutagens that are conserved across host species have a major impact on hantaviruses mutagenesis, contributing to at least six of the 12 possible mutation types. We found differences in mutational signatures across hantaviruses, some of which may be due to variation in host mutagen levels that are known to influence somatic mutations. However, we could find no evidence for differential mutational signatures between viruses associated with distinct diseases in humans and no evidence of tissue tropism differences between reservoir hosts. Using a novel method to quantify the impact of ZAP-mediated selection, we found that ZAP greatly influences mutational patterns in transition mutation types across hantaviruses. We also find evidence that APOBEC family proteins drive mutagenesis in all hantaviruses, with the likely exception of Nova virus. Our results therefore provide strong support that mutagens and host antiviral proteins are major contributors to hantavirus mutagenesis, thereby generating the genetic diversity necessary for viral adaptation.

We 13 currently have a poor understanding of the processes that contribute to hantavirus 14 mutagenesis and therefore the potential for viral adaptation. We found differences in mutational signatures across hantaviruses, 19 some of which may be due to variation in host mutagen levels that are known to influence 20 somatic mutations. However, we could find no evidence for differential mutational signatures 21 between viruses associated with distinct diseases in humans and no evidence of tissue 22 tropism differences between reservoir hosts. Using a novel method to quantify the impact of 23 ZAP-mediated selection, we found that ZAP greatly influences mutational patterns in transition 24 mutation types across hantaviruses. We also find evidence that APOBEC family proteins drive 25 mutagenesis in all hantaviruses, with the likely exception of Nova virus. Our results therefore 26 provide strong support that mutagens and host antiviral proteins are major contributors to 27 hantavirus mutagenesis, thereby generating the genetic diversity necessary for viral 28 adaptation. 29 Introduction 30 Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that naturally infect hosts within the orders 31 Rodentia, Eulipotyphla and Chiroptera [1–3]. Each hantavirus typically exhibits a close 32 association with one or a small number of host species within which it establishes 33 predominantly asymptomatic infections [3]. For example, Hantaan virus lives within the striped 34 field mouse (Apodemus agrarius), while Andes virus is carried by the long-tailed pygmy rice 35 rat (Oligozomys longicaudatus) [2, 4]. This host association results in most hantaviruses 36 exhibiting strong geographical restriction, determined by the range of their host [1, 3]. The 37 exception is Seoul virus which infects black rats (Rattus rattus) and brown rats (Rattus 38 norvegicus) and correspondingly exhibits a global distribution concomitant with that of its hosts 39 [2]. 40 41 Hantaviruses are capable of infecting multiple cell types, including endothelial cells, epithelial 42 cells, macrophages, follicular dendritic cells and lymphocytes and can be detected in multiple 43 tissues within their reservoir hosts including the lungs and kidneys [3, 5]. Within humans, 44 hantaviruses can cause two distinct diseases, which are associated with different viruses and 45 therefore geographical regions [1, 3, 6, 7]. Human hantavirus cases in Eurasia are associated 46 with Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), while those in the Americas are 47 associated with Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS; also called Hantavirus 48 Cardiopulmonary Syndrome or HCPS) [6, 7]. 49 50 Human hantavirus infections predominantly occur through inhalation of secretions from the 51 major host species, including faeces, saliva and urine [6, 7]. More rarely, infections can occur 52 through bites [6]. Andes virus is currently the only hantavirus with documented human-to- 53 human transmission; such events are associated with close contact and can lead to small 54 clusters of cases [8, 9]. However, zoonotic transmission events are frequent enough to lead 55 to an estimated 10,000 to 100,000 human hantavirus cases each year with an estimated 56 fatality rate of <1% to 40% depending on the virus and outbreak [6]. 57 58 Hantaviruses are within the genus Orthohantavirus and the Bunyaviridae family and as such 59 have a negative sense single stranded RNA genome [10, 11]. The genome is organised into 60 three segments, termed large (L), medium (M) and small (S), of which the M segment encodes 61 the viral glycoproteins Gn and Gc [10]. The substitution rate of hantaviruses is estimated to be 62 in the range of 10-4 to 10-2 substitutions/site/year, typical of RNA viruses [12]. This high 63 substitution rate suggests that hantaviruses are capable of rapid adaptation. 64 65 Adaptation relies on the generation of diversity and therefore on mutagenesis. To understand 66 microbial adaptation, we therefore need an understanding of the mutational processes that 67 contribute to mutagenesis. However, we currently have a poor understanding of these factors 68 within hantaviruses and therefore the processes that may assist or constrain hantavirus 69 adaptation. We and others have recently demonstrated that mutational signatures (context- 70 specific patterns of nucleotide substitution initially applied to detect the drivers of 71 tumourigenesis [13–16]) can identify active mutational processes in microbes [17–26]. We 72 have applied these methods to identify both intrinsic mutational processes encoded by the 73 microbe and extrinsic lifestyle-associated mutagen exposures [18–20, 22]. In this study, we 74 examine and compare mutational patterns across hantaviruses to identify mutational 75 processes that may contribute to hantavirus adaptation. 76 Results 77 78 Mutagens impact hantavirus mutagenesis 79 We calculated single base substitution (SBS) mutational spectra for 14 hantavirus species that 80 exhibit at least 600 sampled mutations [27] amongst M segment genetic sequences (Figure 81 1, Table S1, see Methods). We additionally carried out “tree rescaling” of each spectrum by 82 sequence composition across the respective phylogenetic tree [22]. The overall mutational 83 spectrum is highly similar across viruses at the overall level (median cosine similarity 0.978; 84 Figure S1), supporting conservation of most mutational processes. We found that, as 85 expected, each spectrum is dominated by transition mutations (median 76.7% unscaled, 86 78.1% tree rescaled; Figures 1, S2). In contrast to SARS-CoV-2 [19, 26] and influenza A virus 87 [22], T>A and A>T are typically the most common transversion mutations by raw count (Figure 88 S2). However, following tree rescaling, G>T mutations occur at a similar rate to T>A and A>T 89 mutations (Figure S2). 90 91 92 Figure 1. Mutagens influence hantavirus mutagenesis. (A) Cladogram of the evolutionary 93 relationships between the 14 analysed hantaviruses. The heatmap shows the respective host 94 family, host order, associated human disease (where known) and geographical distribution of 95 each virus. Tip labels include the virus name and, in parentheses, the common English name 96 and scientific name of the respective predominant host species. (B) The SBS mutational 97 spectrum of Seoul virus is shown as proportions of raw mutation counts (left hand panel) and 98 as the proportion of mutations within the tree rescaled spectrum (right hand panel). Asterisks 99 in the right hand panel show C>T and G>A mutations that remove ZAP-associated CG 100 contexts. (C) Comparison of symmetric mutation types in tree rescaled mutational spectra. * 101 shows randomisation P < 0.05, supporting a significant difference from a ratio of one and 102 therefore an elevation of one mutation type over the other. This supports a divergence from 103 equal rates that would be expected under polymerase errors alone, and therefore supports 104 the action of one or mutagens. (D) Comparison of contextual patterns between A>T and T>A 105 mutations in tree rescaled mutational spectra. Each point shows the same mutational context 106 in each mutation type, for example A[A>T]C and A[T>A]C. Points show median values across 107 the eight hantaviruses with at least 160 A>T mutations and at least 160 T>A mutations; this 108 filtering is applied to ensure there are sufficient mutations to compare contexts [22]. The 109 significant positive correlation between non-symmetric contexts supports the action of one or 110 more mutagens that causes A>T and T>A mutations with the same surrounding context 111 preferences. 112 113 We next tested for the impact of mutagens by comparing the relative rates of symmetric 114 mutation types [22] and found evidence of mutagens causing G>T (median 2.6-fold elevation), 115 G>A (median 1.3-fold elevation), A>G (median 1.3-fold elevation) and T>G (median 1.6-fold 116 elevation) mutations (permutation test P < 0.05, Figure 1). We previously found evidence of 117 mutagens causing G>T, A>G and T>G mutations in influenza A virus [22], which indicates 118 either common mutagen exposures between the viruses or exposure to distinct sets of 119 mutagens that induce similar mutational patterns. Conversely, we did not find evidence of a 120 mutagen causing G>A mutations in influenza A virus [22], which indicates that hantaviruses 121 are exposed to at least one mutagen that does not influence influenza A virus. 122 123 As T>A and A>T mutations occur at roughly equal rates after tree rescaling (Figure 1, Figure 124 S2), their elevation relative to SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus may be due to either the 125 hantavirus polymerase making more errors between A and T nucleotides, and/or elevated 126 exposure to mutagens that cause A>T and T>A mutations. To distinguish between these 127 possibilities, we examined the contextual preferences within these mutation types. If 128 polymerase errors are responsible, A>T and T>A would exhibit symmetric contextual 129 preferences [19, 22]. However, we observe only a weak correlation between symmetric 130 contexts (Figure S3). Conversely, we observe a strong correlation between the same contexts 131 in A>T and T>A mutations (for example, A[A>T]C and A[T>A]C; Pearson’s R = 0.93, 132 randomisation P < 0.001; Figure 1). Both mutations typically occur most frequently in CXG 133 contexts (where X represents the mutated base) and occur very rarely in XT contexts (Figure 134 S4). This strongly supports exposure to one or more mutagens that introduce A>T and T>A 135 mutations at similar rates with the same contextual preferences. This further suggests that the 136 elevation of A>T and T>A mutations in hantaviruses compared with influenza A virus and 137 SARS-CoV-2 is due to mutagen exposure rather than polymerase errors. 138 139 Drivers of differences in mutational patterns across hantaviruses 140 We next examined drivers of variation in mutational patterns between hantaviruses. We 141 initially tested for an impact of viral evolutionary history and found no evidence that the 142 proportion of any mutation type follows the hantavirus phylogenetic tree (continuous 143 association index P > 0.05 in each case; Figure 2). This indicates that viral genetic factors 144 have limited direct impact on the mutational spectrum and therefore suggests that variation 145 between viruses predominantly arises from extrinsic factors. 146 147 148 Figure 2. Variation in mutational spectrum across hantaviruses. (A) The cladogram 149 shows the phylogenetic relationships between the 14 analysed hantaviruses [2]. Mutation 150 types are shown as proportions within the respective spectrum and proportions are normalised 151 so each column runs from zero to one. (B) Principal component analysis of seven hantaviruses 152 with known human disease associations (Table S1) based on mutation type proportions. 153 Viruses do not cluster by associated human disease. (C) The proportion of G>T mutations 154 within the tree rescaled spectrum is shown for each hantavirus. 155 156 We further found no evidence that differences in mutational spectra are associated with host 157 order or host family (ANOVA P > 0.05, Figure S5), or that any mutation type follows the host 158 phylogeny (continuous association index P > 0.05, Table S2). This suggests that the 159 hantavirus mutational spectrum is not greatly influenced by host factors that are conserved at 160 the level of host family or host order. 161 162 We next tested whether there is evidence of differential mutational spectra between 163 hantaviruses associated with distinct disease in humans. We found no separation of viruses 164 associated with HFRS from those associated with HPS when clustering based on mutational 165 patterns and observed no mutation types that differ by associated disease (ANOVA P > 0.05; 166 Figures 2, S6). This suggests that differences in human disease between viruses are not 167 driven by alternative tissue tropism within the reservoir species. 168 169 We next examined variation in the level of G>T mutations across hantaviruses, which we have 170 previously found can be associated with replication sites in RNA viruses and bacteria [18, 19]. 171 We found that the level of G>T mutations varies markedly between hantaviruses, from 1.8% 172 of mutational burden (accounting for genomic composition) in Khabarovsk virus to 9.5% in 173 Thailand virus (Figure 2). This variation may be driven by differential replication site 174 preferences in different viruses and/or by distinct mutagen levels across host species. Cao Bang virus is not an outlier for other mutation types, suggesting that this is not 202 due to reduced ZAP-mediated selection. We find a significant correlation between the 203 magnitude of ZAP enrichment in G>A mutations and the C>T/G>A symmetric mutation type 204 ratio (permutation test P < 0.05 including and excluding Cao Bang virus; Figure S8). This may 205 indicate that hantaviruses with reduced ZAP enrichment in G>A mutations are more exposed 206 to an additional mutagen driving G>A mutations under different contextual preferences, which 207 reduces the overall enrichment of ZAP-associated contexts. 208 209 210 Figure 3. Influence of host ZAP and APOBEC family proteins on hantavirus 211 mutagenesis. (A) We developed a ZAP enrichment score that calculates relative ZAP activity 212 through the enrichment (for mutation types that remove ZAP contexts) or suppression (for 213 mutation types that introduce ZAP contexts) of ZAP-associated contexts. This score was 214 calculated for each mutation type in each virus that contains at least 160 mutations within the 215 respective mutation type (see Methods). The distributions of these scores are shown for each 216 mutation type. T>A and A>T mutations are not included as they do not introduce or remove 217 ZAP contexts. C>A, C>G, G>C, G>T and A>C are not shown as they contain a maximum of 218 two viruses with at least 160 mutations. (B) The proportion of C>T mutations with each 219 upstream nucleotide in tree rescaled spectra. * shows permutation test P < 0.05 comparing 220 the distributions of T[C>T] mutations with those of the other upstream nucleotides. 221 222 We do not find evidence that any hantavirus exhibits consistently higher ZAP activity across 223 mutation types, or of consistent elevation of ZAP activity within a host family (Figure 2). Volume 32, Number 10—October 2026 Dispatch Characteristics and Superspreading Potential of Andes Virus Person-to-Person Transmission Suggested citation for this article Abstract By using historical contact tracing data, we estimated that 23.4% of case-patients caused 80% of Andes virus (ANDV) person-to-person transmission. We demonstrated a low but nonnegligible probability of observing a large-scale ANDV infection outbreak in a rodent-free setting consisting of close contacts, despite the historically self-limited person-to-person transmission of ANDV. Hantaviruses are rodentborne zoonotic enveloped RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae (1). The genus Orthohantavirus, which belongs to the subfamily Mammantavirinae, is the only genus in Hantaviridae that can cause disease in humans (1). Infections in humans occur mainly through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, which can lead to hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, a severe respiratory disease with a case-fatality rate of up to 50% in the Americas, depending on the infecting hantavirus type (2). Although uncommon, person-to-person transmission of Andes virus (ANDV), a member of the genus Orthohantavirus, has been documented in South America in recent decades, typically in high-intensity close-contact settings, such as households and social gatherings (3–9). On May 2, 2026, an ANDV outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship was reported to the World Health Organization (WHO), with the first case illness onset on April 3 (10). Subsequent epidemiologic investigations proposed a working hypothesis that person-to-person transmission originated from a seed case in a person who probably acquired infection through environmental exposure during travel in Argentina before boarding the ship on April 1 (10). By July 2, a total of 13 ANDV cases had been identified, including 12 laboratory-confirmed and 1 probable case; 3 of those cases were fatal (10). According to the initial WHO notification for the outbreak on May 2, public health and control measures, including contact tracing, case isolation, clinical care, and medical evacuation of symptomatic passengers, had been implemented onboard the ship (11). By using historical contact tracing data, we aimed to estimate key epidemiologic characteristics of person-to-person transmission of ANDV, including the serial interval (SI) distribution and transmission heterogeneity, given that those traits strongly shape outbreak size. We conducted a literature review of historical ANDV outbreak investigations and extracted contact tracing data from ANDV case clusters that involved person-to-person transmission events. We only included studies conducted in Argentina, given that the seed case-patient of the 2026 outbreak was most likely infected there, according to the WHO report (10). We identified 5 eligible studies that provided detailed contact histories and viral genetic evidence strongly supporting person-to-person transmission and linking infections to specific viral lineages or strains (3–7). We extracted symptom onset dates to calculate the SI and compiled case-cluster sizes to estimate the effective reproduction number (Rt) and transmission heterogeneity measured by a dispersion parameter (k) (12). In case-clusters, we considered terminal cases and sporadic cases attributed to environmental exposure but with no documented human contact as generating no secondary infections. We used a Bayesian hierarchical model to estimate the epidemiologic parameters while accounting for random effects attributable to epidemiologic differences among ANDV lineages or strains during different epidemic periods. We further conducted a branching process simulation study to assess the transmission potential of the current outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise ship on the basis of the pooled estimates of epidemiologic parameters, considering a plausible range of the initial Rt for ANDV (Appendix). We identified a total of 88 case-clusters from the included studies, among which 50 (56.8%) were not associated with any secondary person-to-person transmission events. After accounting for variations across lineages or strains, the pooled estimate of Rt was 0.74 (95% credible interval [CrI] 0.28–1.29) and the estimate of k was 0.64 (95% CrI 0.36–1.16). Apart from inherent differences among ANDV lineages or strains, the substantial variation in Rt across lineages or strains could also be attributed to differences in study settings and individual-level heterogeneity in reproduction numbers (5). We estimated that 23.4% (95% CrI 15.1%–30.3%) of the cases generated 80% of the transmission events, suggesting the person-to-person spread of ANDV exhibited relatively high heterogeneity, although it appeared lower than that observed for other pathogens known for superspreading events, including SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus, and Ebola virus (13,14). Among 38 case-clusters that involved secondary transmissions, we identified 76 primary–secondary transmission pairs with available symptom onset dates, which enabled us to calculate the SI. We estimated a pooled mean SI of 21.92 (95% CrI 18.97–25.78) days and an SD of 6.98 (95% CrI 5.80–8.66) days. Although we observed little variation in the SI distributions across lineages or strains, our estimates are conditional on reported case-clusters and might not represent the full population-level distribution of ANDV infections. That condition is particularly relevant given that only 1 transmission pair was identified for the ANDV Cent BsAs lineage (Figure 1). Assuming the initial reproduction number of the current ANDV outbreak lies within the 0.4–2.5 range (3) (Appendix Figure 1), together with the pooled SI and k estimates from historical data, we simulated plausible outbreak trajectories under a stochastic branching process framework. On the basis of the assumption that effective control measures were implemented after the WHO notification dated May 2, 2026 (11), we assumed the Rt decreased from that date onward (Appendix). Within 10 weeks after symptom onset of the seed case, 95% of the simulation results produced <15 cumulative cases of ANDV infection (Figure 2). We estimated the probability of sustained transmission after 1 generation of spread to be 20.9% (95% CrI 5.3%–37.4%) for historical ANDV infection clusters and 28.6% (95% CrI 10.0%–57.4%) using the assumed initial reproduction numbers of the ANDV infection outbreak on the cruise ship (Figure 3). In sensitivity analyses, excluding sporadic cases from historical clusters yielded results similar to those of the main analysis (Appendix Figure 2). The absence or delayed implementation of control measures would increase the likelihood of a large-scale outbreak, under the assumption that such measures effectively reduce the reproduction number (Appendix Figure 3). Because only 8 cases occurred within approximately 1 mean SI after the putative seed case-patient’s symptom onset (18–25 days) before the initial WHO notification on May 2, 2026, conventional methods cannot reliably estimate the initial reproduction number without support of contact tracing data. Nonetheless, we used a branching process simulation model with transparent assumptions to illustrate plausible epidemic trajectories for the ANDV outbreak. We noted that person-to-person transmission of ANDV in the general community might be close to the situations of historical ANDV outbreaks, where we observed mostly self-limited risks. Timely and accurate identification of ANDV infection is critical yet challenging because of the nonspecific nature of early symptoms, which necessitates systematic risk assessment for symptomatic persons and their contacts. A key limitation of this study was its reliance on self-reported contact histories and symptom onset dates derived from publicly available data sources. Potential misclassification of epidemiologic links attributable to unreported co-exposures to rodents, underdetection of subclinical or asymptomatic infections caused by terminal cases, and recall bias in symptom onset might have affected the parameter estimates (15). Of note, no clear evidence supporting transmission from asymptomatic or presymptomatic case-patients currently exists. In the simulation study, we anchored control measures to the symptom onset date of the seed case-patient, thereby overlooking the biological delay imposed by the incubation period. In summary, our results provide insights into the person-to-person transmission potential of ANDV, which exhibited substantial heterogeneity. We found a low but significant chance of observing a relatively large-scale ANDV outbreak in a rodent-free setting consisting of close contacts, which might be eradicated across a few generations of person-to-person transmission. Because no vaccine or antiviral treatment for ANDV infection is currently available, continuous surveillance of person-to-person transmission risk of ANDV is essential for preparedness against future outbreaks. analysis.methods: The study retrospectively reviewed historical ANDV outbreaks in Argentina, extracted contact tracing data, calculated serial interval, effective reproduction number (Rt), and dispersion parameter (k) using a Bayesian hierarchical model, and performed branching‑process simulations to assess outbreak potential (F14–F22).
analysis.results: Pooled estimates yielded Rt = 0.74 (95% CrI 0.28–1.29) and k = 0.64 (95% CrI 0.36–1.16); 23.4% (95% CrI 15.1%–30.3%) of cases caused 80% of transmissions; mean serial interval was 21.92 days (SD 6.98) (F23–F27). analysis.contribution: These quantitative estimates of transmission heterogeneity and superspreading potential enhance risk assessment and guide control measures for future ANDV outbreaks (F25, F32–F35).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus (ANDV) can transmit between humans, but such events are rare; quantifying transmission heterogeneity and superspreading is essential for outbreak preparedness. Methods: The study retrospectively reviewed historical ANDV outbreaks in Argentina, extracted contact tracing data, calculated serial interval, effective reproduction number (Rt), and dispersion parameter (k) using a Bayesian hierarchical model, and performed branching‑process simulations to assess outbreak potential. Results: Pooled estimates yielded Rt = 0.74 (95% CrI 0.28–1.29) and k = 0.64 (95% CrI 0.36–1.16); 23.4% (95% CrI 15.1%–30.3%) of cases caused 80% of transmissions; mean serial interval was 21.92 days (SD 6.98). Simulations predicted a 95% chance of <15 cumulative cases within 10 weeks and sustained transmission probabilities of 20.9% historically and 28.6% for the cruise‑ship outbreak. Contribution: These quantitative estimates of transmission heterogeneity and superspreading potential enhance risk assessment and guide control measures for future ANDV outbreaks. Limitations: Estimates rely on historical contact tracing data that may not capture all transmission settings; serial interval estimates are conditional on reported clusters and limited for some lineages; simulations assume effective control measures and may not reflect all real‑world scenarios.

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)可在人际间传播,但此类事件罕见;量化传播异质性和超传播对于疫情防备至关重要(F5–F9, A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究回顾性审查了阿根廷历史上的安第斯病毒暴发,提取接触追踪数据,利用贝叶斯层级模型计算序列间隔、有效复制数(Rt)和离散参数(k),并进行分支过程模拟以评估暴发潜力(F14–F22)。
analysis_zh.results: 合并估计得到 Rt = 0.74(95% CrI 0.28–1.29)和 k = 0.64(95% CrI 0.36–1.16);23.4%(95% CrI 15.1%–30.3%)的病例导致了80%的传播;平均序列间隔为 21.92 天(标准差 6.98)(F23–F27)。模拟预测在10周内累计病例数小于15的概率为95%,历史上持续传播的概率为20.9%,邮轮暴发的概率为28.6%(F32–F35)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些关于传播异质性和超传播潜力的定量估计提升了风险评估,并为未来安第斯病毒暴发的防控措施提供指导(F25, F32–F35)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 估计依赖于历史接触追踪数据,可能未覆盖所有传播环境;序列间隔估计基于已报告的聚集且对部分谱系有限;模拟假设有效的控制措施,可能未反映所有真实情境(F28, F34, F35, F36,未在提供的证据中报告)。

papers.title: Spatial-temporal distribution characteristics of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in 31 provinces and municipalities of P.R. China and multi-factorial prediction of incidence
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To integrate multi-source spatiotemporal data and construct an HFRS incidence prediction model using XGBoost with SHAP, exploring factors associated with HFRS incidence in China. METHODS: Collected HFRS case data from 31 provinces in China (2005-2020) and multi-source data on climate, land use, and population. Used MaxEnt to analyze rodent distribution and key environmental variables. Constructed an XGBoost model integrating climate, land use, host, and socio-economic features, with SHAP values assessing feature contributions. Dataset divided into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) sets, with higher weights for high-incidence provinces. RESULTS: The reported HFRS cases in mainland China decreased from 2005 to 2020 but showed seasonal peaks. Cases were mainly among adults aged 20-60 years. The distribution of virus-carrying rodents was mainly affected by minimum temperature of the coldest month and elevation. After removing temporal features, land-use types (forest, cropland, shrub) showed greater relative importance than climate variables. CONCLUSION: Forest, shrub, and cropland may affect disease transmission via host distribution and food availability. Climate factors act indirectly on HFRS risk. Temporal features remain critical for incidence prediction, while land use and rodent habitats are key exogenous drivers. These findings support targeted public health strategies.

Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious rodent-borne infec­ tious disease that remains an important public health concern in China. Although the number of reported HFRS cases has generally declined, the disease contin­ ues to show clear seasonal and geographical differences, making it difficult to identify areas and periods of increased risk. In this study, we combined HFRS surveillance data from 31 provincial-level regions in mainland China between 2005 and 2020 with information on climate, land use, population, and the distri­ bution of virus-carrying rodents. We found that HFRS cases were concentrated mainly among adults aged 20-60 years and showed distinct seasonal peaks. We also identified important differences in the distribution of the two major rodent groups associated with HFRS. Our prediction analysis showed that recent HFRS case patterns were the strongest predictors of future incidence. When previous case information was excluded, land-use characteristics, particularly forest and cropland, became the most important factors, while climate factors appeared to influence HFRS risk partly by shaping rodent habitats. These findings highlight the importance of combining disease surveillance with environmental and rodent monitoring to improve early warning and support more targeted HFRS preven­ tion and control in China. Introduction Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), also known as epidemic hem­ orrhagic fever, is one of the most burdensome rodent-borne diseases globally. Its pathogens, Hantavirus (HVs) or Seoul virus (SEOV), have established stable natural foci across the Eurasian continent [1–3]. These viruses are transmitted to humans through exposure to contaminated rodents or infectious aerosols generated by these animals [4]. Upon infection, patients typically present with symptoms such as fever, headache, myalgia, renal damage, and hemorrhagic manifestations [5]. Among the approximately 60,000–100,000 infection cases reported globally each year, over 90% occur in China [6]. In recent years, the overall number of reported HFRS cases in mainland China has been on a downward trend [7]. This highly aggregated epidemic pattern is closely related to complex ecological environments. The breeding cycles of host rodents (such as Rattus norvegicus and Apodemus agrarius) are driven by climatic fluctuations, while land-use changes influence the probability of host-human contact by altering habitat structures [8,9]. More importantly, China’s vast geograph­ ical differences and diverse climate types make the elimination of HFRS extremely challenging. The known risk factors for HFRS incidence include climate, host population dynamics, and viral epidemiology, with climate being widely recognized as an important factor [12,13]. It primarily affects the prevalence of the virus and the risk of human infection by influencing rodent population dynamics. For example, temperature, humidity, and precipitation affect crop yields, which are a food source for rodents [13,14]. Moreover, the dynamics of rodent population density and Hantavirus infection prevalence are related to contact rates. The virus may become extinct below a certain host density [12,15,16]. Under the context of global warming, the periodic dynamics of rodent populations are changing, and new epi­ demic areas are emerging [17]. There is an urgent need to explore the transmission of HFRS under different climatic con­ ditions [18]. Additionally, human activity patterns, which are influenced by weather conditions and seasonal fluctuations, have a direct impact on human-rodent interactions [19]. Furthermore, there is a positive correlation between population density and HFRS outbreaks. An increase in urbanization rates and gross domestic product (GDP) tends to be associ­ ated with higher HFRS incidence rates. Against the backdrop of global climate change, a thorough understanding of the intricate interactions between various variables and the multifaceted determinants affecting HFRS trends in China could be crucial for effectively mitigating the disease. Thus, we hypothesized that climate conditions, land-use structure, and rodent host distribution jointly and interactively influence the spatiotemporal variation of HFRS incidence in mainland China. Mathematical models have been widely used for predicting disease transmission [5]. However, existing models often focus on single-factor analyses [20]. For example, time-series models based on climatic factors (such as SARIMA) can capture seasonal patterns but ignore long-term effects brought about by factors such as human activities and land- use changes [21,22]. Landscape composition is an important factor in the ecology of the rodent-Hantavirus ecological system [23,24]. Although niche modeling or species distribution modeling can analyze the risks of ecological fragmen­ tation, they struggle to integrate social determinants (such as population movement and urbanization). This “divide and conquer” research paradigm leads to the neglect of key synergistic mechanisms, which may limits the precise alloca­ tion of prevention and control resources. XGBoost is a boosting algorithm that combines multiple learning algorithms to achieve competitive predictive performance than any single component learning algorithm, and it has shown satisfac­ tory performance in many fields [25]. Based on multi-source data from 31 provinces and municipalities in China from 2005 to 2020, this study constructed an XGBoost with SHAP feature framework. This framework integrates the static niche model with the dynamic advantages of machine learning to build a provincial prediction model. Spatial interaction terms were generated, and high-incidence areas were precisely modeled through sample reweighting. SHAP was intro­ duced to parse the model’s decision-making path, enabling visualization of important drivers at the provincial scale and guiding targeted intervention measures. The study also explored the impacts of selected factors and their interactions on HFRS incidence. Results Temporal trends of reported cases and infection status in Mainland China, 2005–2020 From 2005 to 2020, a total of 182,865 cases were reported in mainland China, with the majority of cases concentrated in Heilongjiang Province, Liaoning Province, Shandong Province, Shaanxi Province, Jilin Province, and Hebei Province (Fig 1C). Overall, the reported cases of HFRS in mainland China showed a downward trend but with distinct seasonal peaks (Fig 1A). Notably, a significant peak in reported cases was observed in November and December during the period from 2012 to 2020 (Fig 1A). In terms of the age distribution of reported cases, the incidence was primarily concentrated among adults aged 20–60 years, with the age group of 30-50 years typically experiencing the highest incidence (Fig 1B). Although the overall reported cases decreased, the proportion of reported cases among individuals aged 60 years and above showed a relative increasing trend (Fig 1B). Among the top 20 rodent genera (accounting for 90.8% of all records), the genus Rattus had the highest proportion at 28.2%, followed by the genus Apodemus at 15.9% (Fig 1C, S1 Table). Spatial autocorrelation analysis of these two genera revealed a significant positive spatial correlation in their distributions, indicating strong spatial clustering of both genera in China. However, the degree of clustering was slightly lower for Apodemus (Moran’s I = 0.214, p < 0.05) than for Rattus (Moran’s I = 0.253, p < 0.01). Distribution and ecological niche prediction of rodents carrying HV/SEOV carriers Among over 7,000 rodent distribution records, 1,640 records of HV/SEOV-positive rodents were identified, mainly concen­ trated in Zhejiang, Shandong, Hunan, and Hebei provinces (Fig 1C). These rodents belonged to 11 genera and 20 spe­ cies, with Rattus norvegicus accounting for the highest proportion (31.7%), followed by Mus musculus (13.7%), Apodemus agrarius, and Rattus flavipectus (each approximately 11%) (Fig 1D). The MaxEnt model achieved an average test Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.896 (S1 Fig). Key influential variables were Bio_6 (Minimum Temperature of the Coldest month, 8.32%), Bio_15 (Precipitation Seasonality, 11.073%), Bio_13 (Precipitation of Wettest Month, 10.79%), and ELEV (Elevation, 61.20%) (S2 Table). Jackknife analysis indicated that elevation appeared to be a strong predictor, while Bio_15 has the weakest predictive ability (S2 Fig). Response curve analysis suggested a negative correlation between elevation and carrying rodent suitability; suitability decreased with increasing elevation (S3 Fig). Virus carriage likelihood increased with Bio_14 (Precipitation of Driest Month) and Bio_19 (Precipitation of Coldest Quarter), and showed unimodal relationships with elevation, Bio_5 (Max Temperature of Warmest Month) and Bio_13 (Fig 2D). High-suitability areas are shown in red (Fig 2B). Construction and SHAP interpretation of the National HFRS prediction model based on multi-source data We developed an XGBoost prediction model integrating multiple features, including climate, land cover, host and social factors using Tweedie regression for zero-inflated monthly case data. Early stopping was applied, with data split into train­ ing (20052016), validation (2016-2017) and test sets (2018-2020). The model achieved an R2 of 0.8006 on the validation set (S3 Table). Feature importance analysis showed that temporal lag variables (annual_trend, case_lag1, and case_lag12) contrib­ uted most prominently, accounting for more than 80% of total contribution. After removing temporal features to evaluate exogenous drivers, the model achieved an R2 of 0.7084 (S4 Table). SHAP analysis indicated that land-use types were major contributors, especially Forest (0.2546) and Impervious surface (0.1456) (Figs 3B, S4). Fig 3C presents the joint effect of case_lag1 and case_lag12 on current HFRS incidence using Generalized Additive Model (GAM). Blue indicates positive effects (higher risk), red indicates negative effects (lower risk). The highest positive effects were observed when both lagged cases were at moderate-to-high levels (600-800 cases). At extremely high values (>1000 cases), the effect became negative, suggesting a nonlinear saturation pattern. Impact of land-use types on major hosts Apodemus and Rattus were primary HV/SEOV hosts. Both genera were positively correlated with cropland and forest pro­ portions (Fig 3D). GAM analysis revealed that Apodemus exhibited a low-promotion, high-inhibition relationship with land-use features, while Rattus showed the opposite trend. The effects of water bodies and shrubland were not significant (Fig 4A-4B). Principal Component Analysis (PCA) analysis showed that among the six provinces, Heilongjiang, Liaoning, and Jilin, were dominated by cropland, Shandong and Hebei provinces by impervious surfaces and water, and Shaanxi by high forest and shrub. China and multi-factorial prediction of incidence Huan Huang1,2☯, Xin Zhao3☯, Jiaojiao Qian2☯, Hengduan Zhang4, Fanjin Meng1,2, Qiyuan Kuai2, Weibo Ma2, Yifan Wu2, Huajing Zhu3*, Weilong Tan 1,2* 1 Department of Epidemiology, School of Public Health, Nanjing Medical University, Nanjing, China, 2 Nanjing Bioengineering (Gene) Technology Centre for Medicines, Nanjing, China, 3 Jinling Hospital, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China,‌ 4 State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity, Beijing, China ☯ These authors contributed equally to this work. * 13815860287@163.com (HZ); njcdc@163.com (WT) Abstract Objective To integrate multi-source spatiotemporal data and construct an HFRS incidence prediction model using XGBoost with SHAP, exploring factors associated with HFRS incidence in China. Methods Collected HFRS case data from 31 provinces in China (2005-2020) and multi-source data on climate, land use, and population. Used MaxEnt to analyze rodent distribu­ tion and key environmental variables. Constructed an XGBoost model integrating climate, land use, host, and socio-economic features, with SHAP values assessing feature contributions. Dataset divided into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) sets, with higher weights for high-incidence provinces. Results The reported HFRS cases in mainland China decreased from 2005 to 2020 but showed seasonal peaks. Cases were mainly among adults aged 20-60 years. The distribution of virus-carrying rodents was mainly affected by minimum temperature of the coldest month and elevation. After removing temporal features, land-use types (forest, cropland, shrub) showed greater relative importance than climate variables. Conclusion Forest, shrub, and cropland may affect disease transmission via host distribution and food availability. Climate factors act indirectly on HFRS risk. These findings support targeted public health strategies. Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious rodent-borne infec­ tious disease that remains an important public health concern in China. Although the number of reported HFRS cases has generally declined, the disease contin­ ues to show clear seasonal and geographical differences, making it difficult to identify areas and periods of increased risk. In this study, we combined HFRS surveillance data from 31 provincial-level regions in mainland China between 2005 and 2020 with information on climate, land use, population, and the distri­ bution of virus-carrying rodents. We found that HFRS cases were concentrated mainly among adults aged 20-60 years and showed distinct seasonal peaks. We also identified important differences in the distribution of the two major rodent groups associated with HFRS. Our prediction analysis showed that recent HFRS case patterns were the strongest predictors of future incidence. When previous case information was excluded, land-use characteristics, particularly forest and cropland, became the most important factors, while climate factors appeared to influence HFRS risk partly by shaping rodent habitats. These findings highlight the importance of combining disease surveillance with environmental and rodent monitoring to improve early warning and support more targeted HFRS preven­ tion and control in China. Introduction Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), also known as epidemic hem­ orrhagic fever, is one of the most burdensome rodent-borne diseases globally. Its pathogens, Hantavirus (HVs) or Seoul virus (SEOV), have established stable natural foci across the Eurasian continent [1–3]. These viruses are transmitted to humans through exposure to contaminated rodents or infectious aerosols generated by these animals [4]. Upon infection, patients typically present with symptoms such as fever, headache, myalgia, renal damage, and hemorrhagic manifestations [5]. Among the approximately 60,000–100,000 infection cases reported globally each year, over 90% occur in China [6]. In recent years, the overall number of reported HFRS cases in mainland China has been on a downward trend [7]. This highly aggregated epidemic pattern is closely related to complex ecological environments. The breeding cycles of host rodents (such as Rattus norvegicus and Apodemus agrarius) are driven by climatic fluctuations, while land-use changes influence the probability of host-human contact by altering habitat structures [8,9]. More importantly, China’s vast geograph­ ical differences and diverse climate types make the elimination of HFRS extremely challenging. papers.title_zh: 中华人民共和国31个省市肾综合征出血热的时空分布特征及多因素发病率预测

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热 (肾综合征出血热) 是中国重要的啮齿动物传播公共卫生问题,由 汉坦病毒 或 首尔病毒 引起,尽管病例数下降,但季节性和地域性风险仍然持续。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究分析了2005–2020年31个省份的肾综合征出血热监测数据,结合气候、土地利用、人口和啮齿动物分布数据,采用 MaxEnt 进行栖息地建模,并使用 XGBoost 模型结合 SHAP 值预测发病率。
analysis_zh.results: 肾综合征出血热病例从2005年到2020年呈下降趋势,但仍出现季节性高峰,主要影响20–60岁的成人;啮齿动物分布受最低温度和海拔驱动,而在排除时间特征后,土地利用类型(森林、农田、灌木)比气候变量更为重要的预测因子。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果表明,土地利用和啮齿动物栖息地是肾综合征出血热风险的关键外源驱动因素,支持将环境与啮齿动物监测与疾病监测相结合,以提升预警和针对性防控策略。
analysis_zh.limitations: 所提供的证据仅限于摘要和部分正文,缺乏预测模型的具体量化性能指标以及对观察到的关联的详细统计分析。

papers.title: Admission-Time Clinicolaboratory Phenotypes for Early Differentiation of Severe Fever With Thrombocytopenia Syndrome and Hemorrhagic Fever With Renal Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Early differentiation of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains difficult in endemic settings. In this single-center retrospective comparative study, we analyzed admission-time demographic, clinical, and laboratory data from 330 hospitalized patients with laboratory-confirmed SFTS (n = 220) or HFRS (n = 110) admitted between May 2023 and November 2025. Compared with HFRS, SFTS showed an older age distribution, female predominance, more frequent neurological symptoms, and a predominantly hematologic phenotype with modest hepatic differences, whereas HFRS showed more prominent urinary manifestations and greater inflammatory and renal abnormalities. Abnormality-based and normalized organ-domain burden analyses supported the same phenotypic separation, with hematologic, renal, and inflammatory domains showing the clearest exploratory differences. Two differentiation models were developed as proof-of-concept tools using the same complete-case data set and internally evaluated by full-process nested cross-validation. The basic and extended models achieved out-of-fold AUCs of 0.975 and 0.971, respectively; the paired difference was -0.004 (95% CI, -0.014 to 0.005; p = 0.404). Adding CRP, albumin, and LDH did not provide consistent incremental predictive value. These single-center findings provide a proof-of-concept framework requiring independent external validation and recalibration before potential clinical application.
